speaker: Brad Smith
title: An interview with Microsoft President Brad Smith
question: In technology policy, how does the regulatory trajectory of digital technology compare to earlier major physical industries?
guest: In so many respects, digital technology has gone unregulated for probably a longer period of time than any important technology since the 1850s. Compared to the automobile or airplanes, everything that resulted from the combustion engine, we saw more regulation. Just think about the world in which we live: foods, drugs, and cars today are all regulated by health and safety standards, and yet digital technology is not. I think it is overdue. That does not mean regulators should be thoughtless or uninformed or fail to think about balance, but we do need a regulatory floor, and it is right to recognize that. By 2030, in so many ways an automobile is going to be a computer on wheels, and an airplane is going to be a computer with wings. Fundamentally, computers, digital technology, and AI will raise many of these safety issues even if they are in a box that is standing still.

points.core: Digital technology remained unregulated far longer than major industrial technologies since 1850.
points.note: Accept: software and computing went much longer without formal regulation than automobiles, aviation, or other post-19th-century breakthroughs. Do not credit: generic claims that tech moves faster than law without the historical contrast.

points.core: Physical industries like pharmaceuticals operate under mandatory baseline health safety floors.
points.note: Accept: food, drugs, automobiles, or aviation are governed by minimum statutory health or safety standards that digital technology historically lacked. Do not credit: generic statements that regulation exists in other industries without noting baseline safety standards.

points.core: Software now directly controls safety-critical physical machines like modern automobiles.
points.note: Accept: cars becoming computers on wheels, airplanes becoming computers with wings, or embedded AI erasing the boundary between software and physical safety. Do not credit: vague references to IoT without linking to physical safety risks.

points.core: Standalone AI systems still create serious real-world harms without moving physical parts.
points.note: Accept: computers or AI running in a stationary server or box can still inflict imminent societal or personal harm requiring regulatory guardrails. Do not credit: generic AI doom or sci-fi scenarios.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Digital technology has followed a broadly similar arc to earlier physical industries such as railroads, oil, automobiles, pharmaceuticals, and telecommunications, but on a delayed and compressed timeline. Those older industries typically grew with little oversight at first, then faced regulation after visible harms and concentrated market power provoked public backlash: antitrust law and the Interstate Commerce Commission for railroads and oil, the FDA after drug and food scandals, and safety mandates for cars in the 1960s.

Digital technology enjoyed an unusually long and deliberate hands-off period. Policies from the 1990s, such as Section 230 in the United States and a general "permissionless innovation" philosophy, shielded internet firms from liability and sector-specific rules, partly because the harms were less physical and less visible than train crashes or tainted medicines.

Since roughly the late 2010s, the pattern has been catching up. The EU's GDPR, Digital Markets Act, Digital Services Act, and AI Act, along with antitrust cases against large platforms in the US and elsewhere, mirror the earlier shift from laissez-faire to oversight. The main differences are that regulation remains fragmented across jurisdictions, relies less on dedicated sector regulators, and struggles to keep pace with fast-changing, borderless products.

points.why: The response explicitly says digital technology went without oversight unusually long compared with earlier physical industries.
quotes: Digital technology has followed a broadly similar arc to earlier physical industries such as railroads, oil, automobiles, pharmaceuticals, and telecommunications, but on a delayed and compressed timeline.
Digital technology enjoyed an unusually long and deliberate hands-off period.

points.why: The response contrasts mandatory automobile safety requirements with the historical absence of comparable sector-specific rules for internet firms.
quotes: safety mandates for cars in the 1960s
shielded internet firms from liability and sector-specific rules

points.why: The response mentions automobile safety mandates without connecting software to control of safety-critical physical machines.
The response mentions less visible digital harms and the AI Act without explaining how stationary AI systems can cause serious real-world harm.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Digital technology echoes the broad regulatory arc of earlier physical industries—such as railroads, automobiles, aviation, and pharmaceuticals—moving from laissez-faire growth and rapid consolidation to public backlash over harms and monopoly power, and finally toward formal oversight. Yet their trajectories diverge sharply in speed, jurisdiction, and enforcement tools.

Physical industries relied on capital-intensive, geographically fixed assets like tracks and factories, giving governments time and tangible chokepoints to establish sector-specific agencies (such as the ICC, FAA, and FDA), ex-ante licensing, and technical safety standards. Digital platforms, by contrast, scaled globally at near-zero marginal cost and evolved faster than legislative cycles, outpacing regulators while crossing national borders effortlessly. Moreover, lawmakers deliberately shielded early internet firms from traditional liability—most notably through U.S. Section 230—prolonging self-regulation while network effects locked in dominant gatekeepers and intangible harms proved harder to measure than physical accidents. Consequently, whereas physical industries stabilized around preemptive safety and public-utility rules, digital governance arrived largely after market entrenchment, relying on reactive antitrust, data-privacy laws, and contested algorithmic oversight rather than clear sectoral standards.

points.why: The response explains why digital oversight was delayed but does not establish that digital technology went substantially longer without formal regulation than earlier major industries.
The response identifies licensing and technical safety rules that physical industries had to meet before operating.
quotes: ex-ante licensing, and technical safety standards
physical industries stabilized around preemptive safety and public-utility rules

points.why: The response mentions automobiles and aviation but never links software control to the physical safety of either.
The response mentions intangible harms without explaining how standalone AI can cause serious real-world harm.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Most scholars and policymakers, such as former FCC chair Tom Wheeler and Microsoft's Brad Smith, argue that digital technology is following the same path as earlier transformative industries, only faster. Railroads, oil, electricity, telephones, automobiles and pharmaceuticals each started with a largely unregulated period of rapid innovation and investment. Consolidation and market power came next, then visible public harms such as monopoly pricing, unsafe products, pollution and fraud. Political backlash followed, and eventually a settled regime of rules: the Interstate Commerce Act, the Sherman Act and Standard Oil breakup, auto safety law, and FDA approval.

Digital platforms were long exempt by design, through Section 230 and light-touch "permissionless innovation." They are now entering that regulatory phase with the EU's GDPR, Digital Markets Act, Digital Services Act and AI Act, along with US antitrust cases against Google, Meta, Amazon and Apple. Many argue the industry is moving from being an exception to being treated as normal.

The differences matter, though. Digital products are intangible, global and fast-changing, and network effects and data concentrate power quickly. Harms like misinformation and privacy loss are harder to measure than physical injuries. As a result, rules made for one jurisdiction struggle to keep up, and the delay between harm and regulation is under unusual strain.

points.why: The response describes a long digital exemption but says digital technology followed the earlier industrial trajectory faster, leaving the required historical comparison unsupported.
The response names auto safety law and FDA approval but does not explain that physical industries must meet baseline health or safety standards that digital technology historically lacked.
The response never links software control of automobiles or other physical machines to safety-critical outcomes.
The response identifies misinformation and privacy loss but does not explain how standalone AI or computing systems can cause serious harm without controlling physical machinery.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Like earlier physical industries such as railroads, aviation, automobiles, and pharmaceuticals, digital technology began with a period of rapid, largely unregulated expansion justified by the desire to foster innovation. In both cases, mounting public harms and market concentration eventually triggered government intervention: just as accidents and monopolies led to agencies like the FAA, FDA, and ICC, concerns over privacy, disinformation, algorithmic harm, and platform dominance have driven modern frameworks like the GDPR, antitrust enforcement, and emerging AI rules.

Yet digital regulation diverges in important ways. Physical industries generally produced tangible, visible harms that spurred clear, sector-specific safety standards and stable oversight bodies. Digital technologies, by contrast, evolve far faster than legislative cycles, creating a persistent "pacing problem." Their harms are often diffuse, informational, or systemic rather than immediately physical, making regulatory consensus harder to reach. Moreover, because digital platforms are borderless and general-purpose, they cut across traditional jurisdictions and economic sectors, resulting in fragmented, overlapping governance rather than the unified, mature regulatory regimes typical of older industries.

points.why: The response describes an initial unregulated period for both groups without saying that digital technology remained unregulated substantially longer.
The response identifies sector-specific safety standards backed by government oversight in physical industries.

Physical industries generally produced tangible, visible harms that spurred clear, sector-specific safety standards and stable oversight bodies.

points.why: The response discusses automobiles and aviation as historical examples without linking software control to their physical safety.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Digital technology is following a familiar regulatory path. Railroads, automobiles, and other major physical industries initially developed under general laws, with industry-specific rules emerging as they became widely used and their risks became clearer. Railroads eventually faced rules on rates and safety, while automobiles prompted licensing, traffic laws, and vehicle safety standards.

Digital technology is moving through a similar shift, with more specific rules on privacy, competition, and platform accountability as digital services become part of everyday life. The difference is speed and reach. A digital service can scale globally and change rapidly, while regulation usually develops jurisdiction by jurisdiction. That makes it harder for rules to keep pace and for governments to coordinate enforcement.

The response identifies vehicle safety standards as industry-specific rules that set baseline safety requirements for automobiles.

automobiles prompted licensing, traffic laws, and vehicle safety standards

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra

Digital technology broadly follows the pattern seen in railroads, electricity, and automobiles. Early policy often encouraged adoption and relied on general laws. As those industries became essential to daily life, concentrated market power and harms such as accidents prompted more specific rules. Digital policy has followed a similar arc, from relatively light oversight toward targeted rules on privacy, competition, and platform accountability.

The main difference is how quickly a digital service can change and reach users across borders. A single software update can alter how a platform operates in many countries at once, while regulators act on different timetables and mostly within national or regional boundaries.
